english: Let $P$ and $Q$ be the $2\times2$ matrices of reflection of the $xy$-plane in the lines through the origin making angles $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, respectively, with the positive $x$-axis. Let $I$ denote the $2\times2$ identity matrix. Then the number of positive integers $n\le 60$ for which $(QP)^{n}+(PQ)^{n}=I$ is
hindi: माना कि $P$ तथा $Q$, $xy$-तल के उन $2\times2$ आव्यूहों को निरूपित करते हैं जो क्रमशः मूलबिन्दु से होकर जाने वाली तथा धनात्मक $x$-अक्ष से $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ तथा $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ कोण बनाने वाली रेखाओं में परावर्तन दर्शाते हैं। माना $I$, $2\times2$ तत्समक आव्यूह है। तब उन धनात्मक पूर्णांकों $n\le 60$ की संख्या, जिनके लिए $(QP)^{n}+(PQ)^{n}=I$ है, होगी
solution: Reflection in the line at angle $\alpha$: $F_{\alpha}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\alpha&\sin2\alpha\\ \sin2\alpha&-\cos2\alpha\end{pmatrix}$
$R_{\theta}$ multiplies like $\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, so by De Moivre $(QP)^{n}=R_{n\theta}$, $(PQ)^{n}=R_{-n\theta}$ and $(QP)^{n}+(PQ)^{n}=2\cos(n\theta)\,I$
solution_full: The reflection of the plane in the line through the origin at angle $\alpha$ with the $x$-axis has matrix $F_{\alpha}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\alpha&\sin2\alpha\\ \sin2\alpha&-\cos2\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ (it fixes $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ and reverses $(-\sin\alpha,\cos\alpha)$).

Multiplying, the $(1,1)$ entry of $F_{\beta}F_{\alpha}$ is $\cos2\beta\cos2\alpha+\sin2\beta\sin2\alpha=\cos2(\beta-\alpha)$ and the $(2,1)$ entry is $\sin2\beta\cos2\alpha-\cos2\beta\sin2\alpha=\sin2(\beta-\alpha)$, by the compound-angle formulas.

Similarly the other entries give $F_{\beta}F_{\alpha}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos2(\beta-\alpha)&-\sin2(\beta-\alpha)\\ \sin2(\beta-\alpha)&\cos2(\beta-\alpha)\end{pmatrix}=R_{2(\beta-\alpha)}$, the rotation through $2(\beta-\alpha)$.

The matrices $R_{\theta}$ multiply exactly as the complex numbers $\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ do: $R_{\theta}R_{\varphi}=R_{\theta+\varphi}$. By De Moivre's theorem $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^{n}=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$, so $(QP)^{n}=R_{n\theta}$ and $(PQ)^{n}=R_{-n\theta}$.
Adding, the sine terms cancel: $(QP)^{n}+(PQ)^{n}=\begin{pmatrix}2\cos n\theta&0\\0&2\cos n\theta\end{pmatrix}=2\cos(n\theta)\,I$.
So the condition is $\cos\dfrac{5n\pi}{12}=\dfrac12$, i.e. $\dfrac{5n\pi}{12}=2k\pi\pm\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ for an integer $k$.
Since $5\cdot5=25\equiv1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24)$, multiplying by $5$ gives $n\equiv\pm20\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24)$, i.e. $n\equiv4$ or $n\equiv20\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24)$.
For $1\le n\le60$: $n\equiv4$ gives $4,28,52$ and $n\equiv20$ gives $20,44$. Hence there are $5$ values.
(Counting $\cos\dfrac{5n\pi}{12}=\pm\dfrac12$ instead would give $10$, and keeping only one residue class gives $3$ or $2$.)
originality_note: New: two reflection matrices in lines at pi/8 and pi/3 compose to a rotation through 5 pi/12, and the count of n <= 60 with (QP)^n + (PQ)^n = I reduces to a congruence 5n = +-4 (mod 24) (way 5). Closest known: 'reflection followed by reflection is a rotation' and powers of a rotation matrix A^n = R(n theta). Different because: the angle 5 pi/12 has order 24, the sum of the two powers is a scalar matrix 2cos(n theta) I, and the count needs a modular inverse.

Matrices as transformations: rotation, reflection and shear

concept_use.Higher integral powers of a square matri: (QP)^n and (PQ)^n are needed for every n up to 60; they are found as R_{n theta} and R_{-n theta}.
concept_use.De Moivre theorem: R_theta behaves as cos theta + i sin theta, so (QP)^n = R_{n theta} by De Moivre and the sum becomes 2 cos(n theta) I.
concept_use.Matrices as transformations: rotation, r: P and Q are reflection matrices; their product is shown to be the rotation through twice the angle between the lines (5 pi/12).

key_step: Recognising QP as the rotation through 5 pi/12, then solving cos(5n pi/12) = 1/2 as a congruence modulo 24.
justification: Two linked ideas: composition of reflections into a rotation, and De Moivre powers turned into a counting congruence. Comparable to the rotation-power reasoning of 2026-P1-Q8 (L3) and the cis-product argument of 2021-P1-Q4 (L3); options allow a check, so not higher.
